extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of moral and political philosophy; legislators, policymakers, and practitioners interested in the methodology of practical reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Characterizing the methodological relation between science and art (practical rules, ethics, policy): how ends are defined by art, how science supplies the means, and what standards govern formation and application of practical rules and maxims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art versus Science distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever speaks in rules, or precepts, not in assertions respecting matters of fact, is art; the imperative mood is the characteristic of art, as distinguished from science (which speaks in the indicative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art issues ‘ought’ statements (practical rules); science issues ‘is’ statements (descriptions/theorems). This distinction determines different methods: ratiocination/syllogism suits cases where rules are fixed (e.g., a judge interpreting law), whereas the legislator or practitioner must go beyond mere syllogism to consider reasons and grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art defines ends; science supplies means
rubrics_metrics.description: The art proposes to itself an end to be attained, defines the end, and hands it over to the science; science investigates causes and conditions and returns a theorem about how the end can be produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art supplies the major premise (that the end is desirable). Science provides the proposition that certain actions will attain the end. Art then examines practicability and converts the theorem into a rule. This ordering implies responsibility: art chooses aims; science evaluates means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete scientific justification before turning theorems into precepts
rubrics_metrics.description: The theorem or speculative truth is not ripe for being turned into a precept until the whole, and not a part merely, of the operation which belongs to science, has been performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If negative conditions (circumstances that would prevent the effect) have not been ascertained, forming a rule prematurely will lead to failure when counteracting causes occur; the remedy is to reopen and finish the scientific investigation to discover remaining conditions before prescribing the rule as a general precept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules are provisional and adapted to ordinary cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules of art do not attempt to comprise more conditions than require to be attended to in ordinary cases; and are therefore always imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For convenience and cognitive limits, practical rules are formed from imperfect theory and target the most common situations. A wise practitioner treats rules as provisional heuristics and refers back to the underlying scientific laws when circumstances permit or when a case appears unusual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioners must consider reasons, not only formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislator (or practitioner who constructs rules) is bound to take into consideration the reasons or grounds of the maxim; the judge, by contrast, once the rule is ascertained, is final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blindly following formulas makes one a pedant and risks error (illustrated by military tacticians defeated by Napoleon or physicians who follow rules at the expense of patients' recovery). Practitioners should examine the theoretical grounds of rules to know when exceptions or modifications are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art includes rules plus necessary speculative propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: An art, or a body of art, consists of the rules, together with as much of the speculative propositions as comprises the justification of those rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete art selects from science the portion necessary to show on what conditions the desired effects depend; these scientific propositions must accompany rules so practitioners know when rules apply and when to revert to scientific analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for intermediate general principles for arts
rubrics_metrics.description: There is need of a set of intermediate scientific truths, derived from higher generalities of science, destined to serve as the generalia or first principles of the various arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After defining the end and the conditions on which it depends, one should survey available resources and embody the result in the fewest and most extensive propositions possible; these constitute the general scientific theory of the art from which practical methods follow as corollaries (example: Monge's theory of Descriptive Geometry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of ends belongs exclusively to Art
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of the end itself belongs exclusively to Art, and forms its peculiar province; the builder's art assumes it is desirable to have buildings, architecture that they be beautiful, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science cannot decide which ends ought to be pursued; ends are normative commitments of practitioners. Therefore, moral and political questions require teleological or practical-reason principles in addition to scientific knowledge of means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of a single ultimate standard of conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be some standard by which to determine the goodness or badness, absolute and comparative, of ends; and whatever that standard is, there can be but one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple ultimate principles existed, conflicts would require another umpire. Philosophers typically seek one universal standard to which all rules and judgments of praise/blame are referred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleological standard: conduciveness to happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The general principle to which all rules of practice ought to conform, and the test by which they should be tried, is that of conduciveness to the happiness of mankind, or rather of all sentient beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill states his conviction that promotion of happiness is the ultimate principle of Teleology: not necessarily the end of every action in every instance, but the justificatory controller of ends and the test for precedence among competing ends. Even virtues that sacrifice immediate happiness must be justifiable by reference to overall happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deducing conduct from universal practical maxims without scientific grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an error to deduce the line of conduct proper to particular cases from supposed universal practical maxims; one must constantly refer back to the principles of the speculative science to be sure of attaining the specific end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The geometrical school error: sweeping practical maxims (e.g., in political journalism) lead to dogmatic deductions that ignore specific conditions and competing ends. Example: arguing a measure should be adopted because it follows from a government principle, without reference to the actual effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider potential conflicts of ends and modifying causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules must account for the possibility not only that some modifying cause may prevent the attainment of the given end by the prescribed means, but that success itself may conflict with some other end which may be more desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical decision-making requires awareness of trade-offs and the relative desirability of ends; rules that ignore such conflicts risk producing outcomes worse than alternative choices. This reinforces the need to consult scientific/theoretical grounds and teleological ranking of ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art arranges truths for practice (synthesis across diverse scientific truths)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art follows the scientific laws only into such of their detailed consequences as have led to the formation of rules of conduct; it brings together from parts of the field of science most remote from one another the truths relating to the production of different and heterogeneous conditions necessary to each effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whereas science traces one cause to various effects, art traces one effect to its multiplied and diversified causes; practical methodology therefore requires synthesizing heterogeneous scientific results into usable methods for producing complex ends.
